Uniform Title: *Kalasaṃkarṣiṇīmatatantraṭippaṇī* Manuscript: NGMCP Manuscript No. 5-817, Reel No. B25/18 Description: Description by Mark S.G. Dyczkowski.

The *Kālasaṃkarṣiṇīmatatantra*, whose colophons state that it extends to twenty-four thousand verses, is closely related to the *Jayadrathayāmala*. The latter was regarded as so significant that it is also titled *Tantrarājābhaṭṭāraka*. It serves as the primary source for the early development of the Kālī tradition, one branch of which evolved into the Krama system of Kashmir. The *Kālasaṃkarṣiṇīmata*—still worshipped in Kerala and Nepal—is the form of Kālī belonging to the Trika and related schools of Kashmir. Despite numerous scribal errors, this short fragment is of great interest to scholars of these traditions. It forms part of a commentary (*ṭippaṇī*) on the *Kālasaṃkarṣiṇīmatatantra*, which primarily treats the *Ādiyāga* (also known as *Ādyayāga*). In this rite, the Goddess is worshipped by advanced Kaula adepts together with their female consorts using sixteen Kaula substances, such as menstrual blood, excrement, onions, and garlic. We note the presence of *gañjana* (marijuana) among these; while well known from Kaula texts after the thirteenth or fourteenth century, it is very rarely mentioned in earlier ones. Abhinavagupta considered the *Ādiyāga* to be such an elevated ritual practice that he reserved Chapter 29 of his *Tantrāloka* for it as a fundamental Kaula procedure (*kulaprakriyā*). Nevertheless, he took care to present it—and indeed all such rites in his other works—primarily as an internal process mirroring the activity of consciousness. This tract is of particular interest as it provides a glimpse of its original external form.

1a) Oṃ, homage to the gurus beginning with Śiva.
The Goddess said:
Out of your grace, please explain the most secret question, which is profoundly hidden and bestows the supreme truth— the Yoginī and the supreme Prāṇa.
Khecarī, Bhūcarī, Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Sākinī, and Hākinī—
this is the supreme life-force of these Yoginīs, transmitted from mouth to mouth.
"O Lord, speak indeed the secret by which this world is deluded—
the seedless-making, the poison-removing, and the self-kindling of fire."

The movement through the channels, the shaking of the *bindu* and *nāda*, the shaking of the body, the movement of the *śakra*, and the manifestation of the light of the Self— these the sages who know the Vedas declare to be the ten signs of attainment (*pratyaya*) in the Śaiva tradition. They consist of the internal and external embracing and the integration of the channels.
It effects killing, eradication, inciting enmity, and transference; indeed, what need is there for much speaking?

It accomplishes the six supernatural powers (*ṣatkarma*). And how is this Vidyā, O Great-Souled One? How is Kalasaṃkarṣaṇī? O God, how is the worship and adoration? How is the Vidyā the supreme goal? And how are the mudrās?
How does the arising from the state of absorption occur? How is the mandala of convention?
How is the instruction of the master? And how does the channel come to be?
How is the Great-Souled One, the Lord of Gods? What is his appearance like, and how so?
O Lord, how is the abode of Soma and Sūrya, and what is the sequence of deities within the body? How is it that the arm is internal, and what is the sacrificial pap (caruka) and its transmission?
The third is both supreme and non-supreme; thus Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī is threefold.
If you are pleased with me, O God, I am your devotee; speak, O Saṅkara!
"Grant me your grace; speak to me, O Lord!
Śrī Bhairava said:
The lotus is most deeply hidden, well-concealed, and supremely wonderful;
it is a secret, profound mystery, the supreme heart of the Khecarī.
Having realized the entire essence of the vital truth, there is nothing that it cannot accomplish,
even through Brahmā and the other causal deities, as well as the moon, sun, fire, and wind.
Listen now to that which has not been told to anyone, including the world-protectors;
I shall declare to you the definitive teaching concerning the causes, beginning with Brahmā.
The certainty shall be declared and that which is to be told.
Listen to this great secret, accompanied by sacrifice and fire-oblation (*yāga-homa*).
Listen to this: worship, adoration, the purpose of recitation and fire-oblation, the sacrificial pap (*caru*), and the conduct (*caryā*).
2a) Just as one brings about the complete rising [of the breath] through the *mayamelāpanā* channel, so too does it become fruit-bearing.
I shall describe, in brief, the most wonderful wheel (*cakra*).
Likewise, descend into the wheel in the terrible Great Forest of the Ancestors (*mahāpitṛvana*). The Forest of the Ancestors is the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*);
it is the heart, the totality of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), and the collection of the eighteen channels (*nāḍī*).
It is the place where the fierce frowning one, the terrifying one, brings about death according to his intent; this is what constitutes the cremation ground. Thus.

Is the *liṅga* itself Hara, or is it the self-arisen *vāṇaliṅga*, or another *liṅga*? Does the *liṅga* abide in a particular location, or is the *liṅga* situated within the womb (*yoni*), or established in the *lambikā*? It abides there in the great tree at your own station;
the tree is the staff of life (*prāṇadaṇḍa*), the bulbous root (*kaṇḍa*), and the base (*mūla*), extending as far as the Great Mountain at the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*).

Likewise in a forest; on a mountain, at the eastern side, up to the end of the sixteen; or at a great crossroads, where the four corners—the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, *suṣumnā*, and *kuṇḍalinī*—are unified. Therein lies the four-cornered [mandala]. Or else, by a great river; for the great rivers are the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, which are the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*.
The place for wearing the outer robe (saṃghāṭī):
2b) There, it is by a river; or in a great wilderness; or at night; or in a wilderness that is desolate and devoid of people, up to sixteen *krośas*.

Without support, of exceedingly fierce form, profound, and bestowing joy; in terrible great battles and greedy for devouring heroes; the death in the great battle is the *maṭaka*. *Maṭaka* means the mind;
it has been made into a morsel for heroic people, that is to say, it has made sounds and other objects into its morsel—the meaning is that it has swallowed sounds and so forth.

Alternatively, wherever strength arises through mental concentration (*chamānasā*), that is the most excellent state where one attains oneness. Having extracted the knowledge (*vidyā*) there, one should perform [the rite] here and there with a sword in hand, O Great Virtuous One.
[This involves] the heroism of holding a sword in hand and the personal courage of the self; it is the most excellent, the best among heroes and non-heroes.
Then Bhairava [is worshipped] in the Yoginī; the eight Yoginīs beginning with Brāhmī, Bharavratā, Asitāṅgī, and so forth.
Then the Vājita [is worshipped]; the Krodha is the Puruṣa. There, one should first perform the worship of Valāmā and the others in that place, according to the [practice] of the Yoginīs.
3a) But the other sixteen are on one side; there, in that former place, he performs the worship according to which method the rows—
superior, middling, and inferior— are rotated by way of the sixteenfold method.
And having performed worship,
she who is the refuge of the world, possessing poison yet bringing awakening,
remained there with supreme devotion and bowed with great effort to the Primordial Goddess.
The movement of the wheel unifies the sixteen [energies]: Brāhmī, Dvākasī, Dhvajinī, and likewise Annajā; Kandukī, Ciñcinī, Pī, Śānakī, Kṣatriyā, Mātaṅgī, Carmacārī, Dhācarī, and Mahāmati.
Śūdrī, Vaiśvī, as well as Vaiśyā, Dhātakī, and likewise Nastakī.
These [goddesses], when worshipped there, are free from the pride of caste;

Brahmāṇī remains in the state of liberation. She performs the ritual bath of the face. There, on the night of the great lineage, she swallows the fourteenfold creation of beings and likewise remains in the form of Night; she creates them once again.
Thus ends [the section on] Brahmāṇī. || 1 ||
3b) He ripens the cause; he performs a formative action (saṃskāra); likewise, he becomes one who destroys [it]. 2.

The one who possesses the banner (dhvajinī) is the umbrella-bearer (chatradharī); she holds the umbrella. The meaning is that she wards off the entire world-system (brahmāṇḍa) with the umbrella. || 3 ||
Likewise, the Antyajās [merge] all causalities into one. Kubjikā, whose form is the Supreme (parā), is licking [all things] as it were;
she cuts down the sword-like [obstacles]. Just as all grass and wood are consumed by fire, so too [is everything] by her.
Just as one who throws a ball (*kaṇḍukī*) looks at the ball as it rises from the ground, so too does the Supreme Goddess Madhyamā look toward the *Kādī* [vowel] as it emerges from the *kanda*.
Just as various forms arise individually from that which is shining forth, so too does the state of agency manifest in diverse ways. || 5 ||
The *ciñciṇī* [nerve] acts as the ear-ornament; it likewise resides within the center of the womb (*yoni*). It remains supported by the *lambikā*.
From the center of the womb up to the end of the *lambikā*, it pervades and causes the nectar-moon to flow down into the *ciñciṇī*.
The washerman removes dirt; merit and sin are likewise [removed]. Verbal, mental, and physical [impurities]—whatever impurity is burned, in that same way one abandons the internal filth.
One's own intellect cleanses what is defiled. || 7 ||
Śaunakī, Khaṭukī, and Ṣaṭkī meditate upon the thirty-six principles (ṣaṭtriṃśattattva), which consist of sound and the other [objects of the senses], as being indivisible. 8.
Likewise, the Kṣatriya king, as a Kṣatriya, sustains the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) within his entire body and sustains the subjects externally. || 9 ||
Why is Mātaṅgī called Kinnamittā? Why is she the Saṅkarṣaṇī of Time (Kāla), the Sound (Nāda), and the Point (Bindu)?
Wherein, like a beast, she perceives even a mere blade of grass as such; thus is she Mānasī. Carmakārī holds the hide; the Goddess Māyā holds the hide, or she is the leather-worker herself. 10.
The female fisherwoman (dhīvarī) and the female boatman (kevaṭī) for what purpose? She casts the net (jālaṃdharayati). She holds the net of illusion (māyājāla) and the snare for fish;

she restrains the movement of the fish through the causes [of karma]. She assumes the form of a bird, a swan (haṃsarūpa), or she is the female fisherwoman who sustains whatever action is auspicious or inauspicious. The Śūdra woman is the bearer of the sword. The moon... [text fragment]

One who desires creation, for the sake of creation, having made the moon— which is the form of the digit of nectar (amṛtakalā)— into the state of a lord (pati), and likewise another into the state of a forest (vana); such is the meaning.
Thus ends [the section on] the Śūdrī. 12.
In the Vaiśyā-veśyā, the five causes—sound, action, Soma, Sūrya, and Agni—reside together in their entirety. Likewise, in the house of the Veśyā, action manifests in the form of the stars. || 13 ||

Regarding "Mālinī": Mālinī brings forth the entire form of the Mother, which is the cause of the flower (*puṣpa*). In the sense of "unfolding" (*unmeṣaṇa*), she is thus the one who unfolds the multitude of flowers. The form [consists of] the two ears and the two nostrils, devoid of the root;
such is the flower, and likewise she is the maker of the flower. (19)

The dancer (nartakī) is likewise the dancer (nartakī) in the form of the vital energy (prāṇaśakti); she is the female dancer (narī). She moves according to the measure of half-time (ardhakālānurūpaṃ matam). She shakes and leaps with stability and horripilation. She is not far from seeing the small mirror nor from hearing. She is devoid of both duality and non-duality, like the entire collection of ear-ornaments. Such is the meaning of "the dancer" (nartakī). 15–16.

When these goddesses are worshipped, they bestow the fruits of all desires. Thus, one who desires specific results should worship them as desired; the Supreme Lord should worship the six paths with the six [mantras].
5a) In the preceding [section], that which is to be explained is the "broken nose" (bhagnanāsikā); because of that, this letter *i* is seen there.
The sequence of the goddesses situated on the side of the moon is to be observed; "broken nose" refers to the word *bhagna*.

The form of the broken crest, the downward-facing heart-lotus, likewise the lotus, the mouth, and the bulb (kanda); again, the letter *repha* is the solar disc (*sūryabimba*), and the letter *ra* is the lunar disc. For what reason does the Sun join with the Moon, and how is it that he enters into the front of the mouth? The letter *i* is seen as the form of the nose; therein the Moon and Sun are perceived.

The two sides are the rays of the moon and the sun; likewise, the two eyes join together internally and externally for the purpose of embracing [all things]. Thus, the nature of the Goddess is attained. This refers to the one with the broken nose (Bhagnanāsikā). 16.
"O Goddess, one should worship these [deities], which bestow the fruits of all desires.
Thus it is said. Having reached those locations there, which are free from depressions and elevations, one worships the place (5b).
The first sequence is the eldest; the second glance is the eldest; the third is the eldest.
The command is the eldest and supreme—whom here would one not worship? Whose sign descends upon him, for him there is worship at the outset;
he should avoid both the low and the high. He who does not reject [anyone] sees the entire universe as composed of all beings.

One should worship him there in the *argha* vessel at midnight; at that time, having offered the *kulakolāṅgula-piṣṭa* (the paste of the *kula*-stalk) at the site of the *kanda*, one worships on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight at the half-watch of night. Having prepared the *argha* vessel with the water of Śiva, one should then worship Gaurī; he will speak the secret.
With the *mahāphalguttha* incense, one should offer a great red *argha* vessel;
with great oil, one should light lamps in every way during the night.

One should offer incense of *pukṣasaṃ*, an offering vessel of great red [substance], and a lamp of great oil. One should present red *karavīra* flowers; by all means, at night, one should maintain the lamp. When the breath flows through the channels, it carries the light. By bathing, wisdom becomes slight; the bulbous flower is for the two ears. Through the state of duality, they are devoid of duality; this is the *tilaka*.
One should cause the heart to wither through equanimity.
Thus are the offerings for the argha vessel. These offerings of the goddesses are both superior and inferior. These are the offerings.
The offerings are both superior and inferior, extending from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
The offerings consist of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—both superior and middling.
O best of heroes, one should cause wine to be offered, as well as things to be licked and drunk.
One should worship Suradeva, the lord of the middle realm. Liquors are of seventeen kinds, consisting of various delicious things to be licked and drunk;

Then, having extracted it, one should bestow the tongue of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-jihvā*) turned upward. Likewise, in the second watch of the night, the seed-syllable of fire (*vahni-bīja*), devoid of the power of passion (*śakti-rāga*), [is placed] at the tip of the tongue.
That; thirdly, first...;
fourth, the moon that has not waned; ... then...
after that; Ḍa; Aiṁ.
The fifth is Caṇḍarāja, and the sixth is Madhu; hear [of them]. You have certainly [uttered] the seed-syllable of Rudra; that indeed is the seventh, O Tongue, which I bestow upon you.

The seed-syllable of Soma; Sa; the eighth mandala; the seed-syllable of Vama; the seed-syllable of Kavi; Na; the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī; [the syllable] Ī; the leader of the ten glorious seed-syllables; the seed-syllable of Aśva joined with Ṇāhuśva; I; EṂ; ṆI; ten, one—these are the eleven syllables; the second...

First: *ka*. Then, joined with the letter after *sa*: *ā*, *aiṃ*, *kā*. The twelve-syllable seed-mantra of Indra is *la* joined with the womb (*yoni*): *aiṃ le*. Having extracted the twelve-syllable [mantra], it consists of fourteen seeds: *ma*. Now listen to the fifteenth: joined with the first letter of the second group (*va*), it is *va*.

Ā | E | CHĀ | Daśamañca (and the tenth mañca) has been fully explained; now hear the sixteenth. The fifth itself is the sixteenth seed-syllable, the power-āvaṃ: HA | ANVAHAHAṂ | A | AIṂ HA | One should worship them together. Khaṇḍinā, Khaṇḍā, Khaṇḍakhaṇḍāṇḍā, Khaṇḍinī, Khaṇḍa, Khaṇḍo, Matā, Kālī.

The Vidyā consists of ten syllables. She who devours the Bindu of Akula, the form of Kāla, abides as the bearer [of the lineage]. The state of the Mistress of Yoga (Yogaiśvarī) exists; the mass of Vidyās is... ha ha, for the sake of giving, merged in the petals. The Vidyā is... ku-rā. Thus, the ten...

7b) There is no worship, no new offering. By the grace of the Guru, those seventy-seven million [mantras] are by their very nature the Father. The end of the mantras has been severed and pinned down; what is the sequence of the worlds?
There is no name in the three worlds that deludes like this one; it is the pacifier of spirits and *vetālas*, and the cutter away of heaps of sin—thus it is said.
Together with the circle of the Mothers (*mātṛcakra*), listen now to these twelve who are accompanied by the Mothers: Śivā, Vegavatī, Māyā, Bhadrakālī, Karaṅkiṇī, Vajrā, Yamajihvā, and Yakṣakarṇā.
Ghaṭodarī, Vāramātā, Ulūkā, and Karaṅkinī—these twelve indeed [constitute] the Dvādaśa.
In the center are all the Krodhas, Kulārodrī, and Grasanā.

O limb, he performs the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; he creates them again. From the navel to the genitals is Bhuvaḥ; from the navels [upwards] is Loka.

In that regard, the meaning is that one should cause the mind to cease. One should cleanse the heart, which consists of bone and is joined with blood; likewise the skin and the bile, together with the hide. The living being moves about; having known this, one should extract the twelfth divine [element].
Twelve divine [months] make one year; this was established by Jabhi.

The sacrificial offering (naivedya) accomplishes the desired Siddhi. I shall now proclaim another mantra that always destroys the three worlds. Even if merely the syllable *Huṃ* is uttered, it is the manifest Kuleśvarī herself; likewise, she slays. In the *Huṃkāreśī*, even a mere glance is the power (*śakti*). *Ā* is Time (*kāla*), and *Mā-tejaścari* is together with *Sosikā*. *Ī* is likewise.
And the *jama* seed-syllable: *ma*. One should join this with the *piṇḍa*. The *piṇḍa* is *ekatraṃ*: *hsīṃ*.

By means of this mantra of five *piṇḍas*, this [is] the five *piṇḍas*: *huṃ phaṭ*. That is given to you. By this method, it moves by itself; it is accomplished through the mouth of the Guru. By this method, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra [are attained].
And Īśvara, who is Sadāśiva,
when worshipped for even a moment, shall cause [the desired fruit] to fall upon one's head at that very instant;
having formed the *adhyekara* mudrā with hollowed palms, it is established at the tip of the mouth.
8b) One should diligently join the thumb and forefinger;
repeatedly moving the tongue within the mouth, one should bend the left foot.
This should first be performed externally, and afterwards one should practice internally.
The hand is turned downward; the heart-center is the enclosure; contraction is established at the tip of the mouth.
The mouth is downward-facing; the bulb (kanda) has entered the womb (yoni); the lotus is well-known as upward-facing. Half—

One should meditate upon the upper half established within the hollow of the *prapuṭīkā* by means of inhalation (*pūraka*). Or, by touching [it] with a counter-clockwise rotation, one raises Kuṇḍalinī. Whatever nature of the Goddess is attained, the thumb is Śiva; the little finger has gone to the Yoni, while the index finger is the nature of the Liṅga.

The vital power, Kuṇḍalinī, moves in the form of wind; she unites the two nostrils, the mind, and likewise the nature of the eyes. When the two lotuses are unified, one attains the true nature (*svarūpa*);
this is the second mudrā. Regarding the term "meditating" (*ādhyāyati*): having placed the two nostrils below and established them at the tip of the mouth.
One joins the two palms facing downward.
[Regarding] the moon-face (mukhacandra): the orb of the face shall dwell at the *dvādaśānta*. Having bent the little fingers and the index fingers...

Both the thumbs are the two [fire-pits]. The index finger is the solar orb; the thumb is the form of fire. The sun is the heart, and fire is the bulb (kanda). The tongue, as the organ of taste, unites with the bulb. From the union of Śiva and Śakti at the time of the occasion of delight, one's true nature is attained. This is the Amṛtamudrā.
This is the mudrā of the Great Hero, which bestows the accomplishment of heroes; if one correctly employs the wrath [mudrā] at the end of the opening, [the goal is attained].
From this [center], one should worship Edadevī; and in the middle, Kṛśodarī.
One should worship Padmā on this twelve-petaled lotus and on the hexagon, until the end of the aeon.
There, one should worship the Mahālaya of the Goddess.
Indeed, it is to be worshipped eternally as the seed-syllable of Soma with the *visarga*.
Furthermore, the letter *sa* of Soma, joined with two *visargas* and two *bindus*, followed by the letter *kha*, all combined into one.

The five *piṇḍas* are offered. The five *piṇḍas* are [marked with] *khphre saḥ* at the end; these should be joined within the interval of the *homa*, and the end of the *homa* is *svāhā*. One should worship in the house itself. The *caru*—whether superior or middling—should be worshipped with great effort as the external offering.
The sacrificial oblation (caru) offered outside is superior, while that offered within the house is middling; the ordinary oblation is to be worshipped with fish and meat.
The meaning is that one should take whatever has been obtained according to one's capacity, even if it be a slight offering.
Thus ends the first chapter, the *Ṭippaṇaka*, in the *Trailokyamohana* section of the twenty-four thousand verse collection of Vidyās, according to the *Kālasaṅkarṣaṇīmata*.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Then, O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall tell you another [mantra] for the region of the ear;
in its power, it is not equal to even a ten-millionth part of all those [other mantras] in the mind.
Vidyā is the second; she is known as Vidyeshī, the other Samayā.
By reciting her even once, a practitioner [overcomes] millions of obstacles.
Now hear this partless (niṣkalā) vidyā, as well as the mālā-mantra.

Listen, O beloved, to the mālā-mantra: having recited it once, it is called "namānamati" because it consists of ten million [syllables]; and that is the meaning of being "partless. One should know the moon first, ending with the Tārā; [it is] seven times seven ṭikās.
10a) *Namaḥ* is considered the word beyond the supreme; *namaḥ*. [The mantra] *caṇḍa 2*, *pada 2*, when recited at the time of the plow-star (*phālakṣa*), yields its fruit.
The name of the *vidyā* bestows the state of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). *Sarvasiddhi* consists of four syllables and four words; thus it is born.

One shall possess the recollection of past births (*jātismara*). From the *Yoginīs*, the word is *vamaḥ*; six syllables (*varṇa*), five words (*pada*); one is liberated from the two-fold murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), and the state of all perfections (*sarvasiddhipada*) should be granted; four syllables, six words; the destruction of an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*) is dissolved. And from the *Mātṛs*, the word itself is [the mantra]; from the *Mātṛs*: three syllables, seven words; it shall extricate one from the murder of a Guru (*guruhatyā*).

Homage to Nityoditāmarda! Eight syllables; eight words. One should cause the approach to the unapproachable to cease. Likewise, the word *nanditāyai*. Four syllables; nine words. The milking of friends is destroyed. And the entire wheel of the family (*sakalakulacakram*). Seven syllables; ten words. There shall be the bursting of the mudrā. Again, the word *nāyakāyai*, [then] *nāyikāyai*. Four syllables.

Pada 11: *pratimāṃ cālayat sadā* (She who always moves the image). O Bhagavatī Caṇḍī, this is the word consisting of six syllables. Pada 12: *vaitālotthāpanam* (The raising of the Vetālas), and likewise the word for Kāpālinī; this consists of four syllables. Pada 13: *khecaratvaṃ ca siddhyate* (And the state of moving through the sky is accomplished); the word *tadyatheti* should be added.

10b) The first section is supreme. Namely: 3 syllables, 13 words; whatever moves or is stationary is accomplished by this. Of the Mātṛkā-section: 56 syllables, 14 words; and the verse begins with the letter *sā*.

There are fourteen words; furthermore, the second mantra-fragment consists of nine syllables, and the subsequent mantra-fragment consists of six syllables—the meaning being "Bhagavatī. Listen, I shall speak after having heard [your request].

The first is to be known as the Illuminator (*dīpaka*): *oṃ hrīṃ mamatpare hrīṃ hara krama*. After that, *hūṃ* is the third, the leader of the seed-syllables (*bījanāyaka*), for it is the seed of life (*jīvabīja*). The first letter is *ā*; thus, *hā*. Situated together in one place, it is called the Earring (*kuṇḍala*). Joined with the Womb (*yoni*) *pheṃ*, *e* is proclaimed as the fifth. Thus.
Phaṃ. Having extracted the seed-syllable of Mandara: Kṣa. Conjoined with the thirteenth vowel: O. Thus: Kṣauṃ. Having extracted Bhīmā(?)-kusa, the seventh is proclaimed: Kroṃ.
And likewise, the seed-syllable *namaḥ* is twofold: *namaḥ*, *namaḥ*. Thus: Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ hīṃ kṣuṃ kṣāṃ.

11a) *Varṇa* 9: This second nine-syllable mantra-section (*mantrakhaṇḍa*), which has been well-expounded, bestows the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*); it causes one to travel in the atmosphere. It [bestows] the state of being a spirit (*bhūtatva*).

He causes [the disciple] to understand, provided he applies it correctly. Thus, having extracted the first letter and the first word, [one obtains] five *visakas* from the third section. I shall speak of another section of praise; O Goddess, I shall likewise extract and declare it. The supreme threefold reality (*tri-tattva*).

The word: the *tritattva* (three principles), the syllable *oṃ*, the supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*). Thus: four syllables (*varṇa*), one word (*pada*). It becomes invisible. The word "Haṃsinī" should be given: Haṃsinī. Three syllables, two words. Whomever [it] favors, for him there is grace; it is the giver of the path to Nirvāṇa. Six syllables, three words. Visible to those who have realized [it].

It exists as the pacifier of uneven calamities, and [the pacifier] of all misfortunes, ill omens, and the afflictions of the states of existence—namely, all misfortunes, ill omens, and afflictions. Ten syllables, six words; it shall destroy ill omens (*ariṣṭa*). Furthermore, there is another word: *dalanī* (crusher).

*dalani* | three syllables, seven words; it accomplishes the *yakṣiṇī*, as well as all calamities. *sarvāpadapadaṃ tathā sarvāpadaṃ* | four syllables, eight words; it accomplishes the elixir (*rasāyana*). *ambodhi taraṇi* | six syllables, nine words; it accomplishes the elixir.
*anyat sakalaśatrukaṃ sakalasatruka* | five syllables, ten words; the meaning is that it causes the death of all enemies.

The word *pramathani*, O Goddess, consists of four syllables and eleven feet; it is effective for subduing and is always successful. "Come, go indeed"—*āgaccha* twice consists of six syllables and twelve feet; it causes the foot-ointment to take effect. Likewise, the pair of *hasa* syllables consists of eight syllables and thirteen feet; it is the laughter of *vāgbhava*, a poetic composition.

Perform it! Then... [the syllable] ending in *nara-rudhira* (human blood) at the step; likewise, [the syllable] ending in *nara-rudhira*. Six syllables, fourteen steps; it effects the movement of the aggregate (*piṇḍa*). Five syllables and fifteen steps for the eating of fat (*vasā*).
For the initiate (*samayī*), the son (*putraka*), and the practitioner (*sādhaka*), [it is applied] at the step ending in *ār*. Whatever form is made, its bank... [is established].

12a) [The goddess] consumes flesh, fat, and blood; she gives back my sound: "Mama" (mine). [She utters] the color twice, the word six times. She causes [the practitioner] to go to the three worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—and she shall uplift his own kingdom.

Afterwards, [the syllable] * * *? is that word. The sound "bhā" is repeated twice; seven syllables, seventeen words; there occurs the piercing of sensation. Then the word "lāṃ hi" twice, and another word; [seven] syllables, eighteen words; it subdues deaths. Then, with the trident, split the word in two, O auspicious one, with the trident.

Bhindi bhindi! Two syllables; nineteen words. He engages in debate with *khaṃ*. And again, with the sword, he strikes the word. Strike, strike with the sword! Nine syllables; twenty words. The sword-attainment remains. It transcends that; it causes [the target] to go into the sky; it cuts it.
That is the word. One should cut it. Six syllables, twenty-one words. It cuts away eighteen fevers. As long as [one recites] my word and another word... so long, indeed, is it Brahma.

12b) Six syllables; twenty-two words. It becomes a means of subjugation (*vasīkaraṇa*). Every single word, as well as one's desire—every single desire—[is fulfilled]. [The remaining portion of the verse is: *tā pada 2*.
O King, Manoramā brings [them] under control; she accomplishes it. With two lines and the supreme word "O Compassionate One," accomplish it. *?rama kā*?śa*. Thirteen syllables, twenty-four words.
It pacifies the region of the city. And there is another, the Blessed Lady (Bhagavatī). O Blessed Lady! Four syllables, [twenty-four] words.

Namitaṃ. Eight syllables, twenty-seven words; one should bestow the Yoginī-ga[da]ya. Furthermore, all other sounds and likewise the words of the Mantramāja. [Omission]. Seven syllables, twenty-eight words; by "namo namati," the Koṣṭhī-mantras are accomplished.

13a) And the word *praṇatajana* (one who bows to people), as well as the word *vatsatva* (the state of being a child/calf); [the phrase] *praṇatajanavatsale* (O you who are affectionate toward those who bow). [This consists of] 9 syllables and 29 words.
Whatever [there may be] among the gods, asuras, nāgas, vidyādharas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, humans, or even the descendants of Vālmīki...
And the description:
O Goddess, one should utter the word *mahādevi*, [then] *mahākāla*, [then] the term *mahākālanāśini*, [and finally] *mahākalikālanāśini*. There are eleven syllables and thirty words.

The severing of the bonds occurs. And the *haḍama* is threefold everywhere: *huṃ huṃ huṃ*. The syllable (*varṇa*) should be joined with the letter *ā* and the *bindu*; one should employ the supreme body. [She is] tranquil, yet afflicted by passion. Eight syllables; thirty-two words. One should pierce the stone; one should pierce it from the front. "Kuru kuru" should be joined twice. "Kuru" twice; four syllables.
Verse 33: The tearing apart of the machine of the crooked limbs; accompanied by the feet of the gods and asuras;
in the sequence, there is an elision (*lopa*). [The rest of the verse is lost.]

End with Varuṇa (va) together with the bindu (ṃ); [then] the syllable ĀḤ accompanied by Gu (gu). Thus is Śrī. Place Tiṭibhā (ṭi) endowed with all Māyā (hrīṃ). And there are two hundred and more castes who rejoice.
This garland-mantra is indeed remembered as the bestower of all accomplishments;
whatever there is, whether moving or unmoving, is accomplished through it.
In these tantras, within the *Jayadratha* [system], the goddess Siddhilakṣmī exists;
there is no other knowledge equal to her, for she is auspicious and performs all rites.
This knowledge is declared to be great; it is remembered as the *mālā-mantra* of the Gaṇas.
It is not to be given to the unqualified, for it is illuminated by its own inherent nature.

The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the supreme recitation (japa),
which is applied to the path of sound (nāda) for the Śakti intent upon recitation and meditation.

What kind of recitation does he perform as recitation? He performs the recitation by counting up to one hundred thousand. What is meditation like? Therein, one should not recall anything at all regarding the collection of instruments or the mantra;
that which one should not recall, one should recall with the body. One should not recall shame, suspicion, or fear. This is the state of being like a piece of wood.

14b) Free from cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, and devoid of conceptualization, there would be no meditation whatsoever. Furthermore, what else [is there] within one's own body, from the *kanda* up to the *kuṇḍalinī*, and from the *kuṇḍalinī* up to the filament (*keśara*)?
But from the region of the ears and the hairline, it is situated at the throat and between the eyebrows.

From the *bhrūṇa* (the space between the eyebrows) to the *dvādaśānta*, and from the *dvādaśānta* to the *ṣoḍaśānta*, one should fashion the nine syllables in the form of a coil (*kuṭilākārā*). Like a serpent, it is coiled; from the crooked, from the inaccessible, it forms the nine syllables. One should fashion the nine gates. That which is encapsulated is the fire (*kova*); the coiled one at the root (*kanda*) cooks.
From the heart to the throat; from the throat to the middle of the eyebrows;

from the middle of the eyebrows to the dvādaśānta (the twelve-finger space above the head); from the dvādaśānta to the ṣoḍaśānta (the sixteen-finger space). Beyond that, it remains in the supportless state (*nirālamba*). Very gradually, the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*) becomes exceedingly subtle.

Just as at the time of its emergence, one should likewise visualize a pure, stainless crystal blazing with fire. Furthermore, it is like an *indragopaka* insect, having emerged from the cavity of the palate.
By means of the application of the *brahmanāḍī*, one should contemplate the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*).
"Indragopa" refers to the mind. Space extends to the end of the twelve [fingers]. The term "indragopaka" denotes the five sense organs.
It is the pervasion of that conscious mind by sound and the other [objects of sense]. By the word "indragopaka," the host of lights is meant.
Space is perceived. Having emerged through the cavity of the palate, it reaches the *pātāla* (subterranean realm) of the sound of the palate. The cavity (*randhra*) is at the end of the nine;

therein is the end of the sixteen, upward, half-upward, and further upward. As long as one is fixed within the *kanda*, it then rises to the end of the twelve, reaching the form of a flame in the *brahmanāḍī*.

By means of yoga, one should pierce the Brahma-nāḍī, the Suṣumṇā, in the center, through the solar disc, very gradually, until it is unified with the lunar disc by means of the three [channels]. The seven apertures are: the left ear, the left eye, the left nostril, and the Brahma-hole;
the right nostril, the right ear, and the Brahma-door.
Then, [visualizing] this stone on one's head emitting flames,
the yogi should thus restrain the mind there, just as the moon is full.
In this very [context] is forbearance; this is meditation. And I shall explain the external [practice], as well as the *samaya* and the mantra itself.

Through one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpa*), the practitioner who is devoted shall attain success according to his desire. One hundred thousand recitations: the end of the hundred thousand;
at the *akanda*, the face, the station of Brahmā, and the navel, the station of Viṣṇu—this is marked by fire wherever it may be.

The mind, having come to rest, performs a hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpa*). As long as the state of fullness [persists] within the marrow and the solar [channel], I bow to that which is motionless yet vibrating, having merged into the Supreme Reality. From this hundred-thousand-fold recitation:
If he is initiated twenty-seven times, he will become [successful].
From one hundred and eight recitations, he clearly obtains objects of enjoyment.
By seven hundred and eight recitations, there is the destruction of great fear.
Having recited it one thousand times, that great Daṇḍanāyaka [is summoned].
By reciting it eight thousand times, one attains a kingdom at that very moment; or else, by ten thousand recitations, the state of divinity is proclaimed.
Having recited the Rudra-mantra twenty thousand times, one becomes worthy of my grace.
Likewise, O Sadāśiva, by reciting it three hundred times one attains lordship;
likewise, by reciting it eight hundred times, the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva) arises.
Likewise, by reciting it ten times, one becomes equal to the name of the Goddess;
as is the Goddess, so shall he become equal to me within my own body.
Keeping the head and neck level, one should remain motionless;
looking at the tip of the nose, one should not glance toward the directions.
Having performed the fire sacrifice with a tenth part [of the recitation], one should perform the unsurpassed recitation;
having joined it with the letter "ma," that which was done is accomplished according to one's own will.
The sacrifice was performed at the very beginning, having first gathered the sacrificial animals;
it was carried out while fainting [in ecstasy], with a mind intoxicated by the bliss of wine.

Desiring success, they first take up that which is beautifully adorned with the five jewels through the examination of what is concealed and unconcealed; thereafter, they perform the supreme recitation.
One should perform it in a cremation ground, or under a solitary tree, or at a crossroads,
or on a mountain peak, by a riverbank, or in an empty house.
One should perform this recitation and thereafter practice meditation;
[the sites are] the cremation ground, the *kaṇḍu* tree, and up to the sixteenth [tattva].
The crossroads are the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*.
To the east, between the eyebrows, is the empty chamber, the *suṣumnā*. The heart is the mind; the rivers are the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*.
They perform recitation (*japa*) upon this. What kind of external meditation (*dhyāna*) should one meditate upon? The terrible, supreme, and fearsome.

One should meditate on the form of the Goddess who has six faces, three eyes, and thirty-six arms; she is endowed with weapons and bestows success. She is terrible and fearsome in appearance. One should meditate on her as having six faces, thirty-six arms, and three eyes. She is to be meditated upon by the Yoginīs as Mahāyogeśvarī, whose form is like that of Kāla at the time of universal destruction.
Lokaracchī is declared to be in the north; Krodhanīyāśvī is my *dhā*.
Vyomavāmā is above, and likewise Bhāseśvarī is called Nākhya.
One should employ [these] in the upward-facing [direction]; thus is the Khaḍvaktra described.
A ĀḤ! The devouring of time; the fall of hail, the fall of lightning, the fall of thunderbolts;
the fall of upward-moving power, the fall at the end of the maiden, the fall of the great dissolution.
Thus it is established that they cause [the syllables] to fall for the seventh time.
The first ball, having reached the state of falling, becomes five-syllabled.
The second is situated in the state of *myāta*; the third is designated as *pāta* and is proclaimed as ninefold;
the fourth is reached through *nimitta* and is remembered as thirteen in number;
the fifth is likewise situated, while the seventh is pervaded by the regions (*deśa*); and the sixth is pervaded by *pāta*, which is both the signified and the signifier.
It is excluded. On the eastern face, however, is Yogeśī; in the word "yoga" [it becomes] Yogeśvarī. Oḍyāna-pīṭha.

Khphreṃ is the form of withdrawal (saṃhāra). Therein, from the center, is the five-fold mass (pañcapiṇḍa); and the origin of the Lord is the oral tradition of the Guru. On the second face is Sakaṣaṇī; on the southern face is the syllable Klīṃ.
Jālandhara is the sacred seat (pīṭha). The third is the northern face. Karaṅkiṇī is the eastern seat.
The goddess Kubjikā is born from the syllable Śrī. The fourth is the western face; the goddess Krodhinī is... [kā * *##? 17b)

The goddess Vāmeśvarī is born from the syllable Aiṃ. Above that, in the Inexplicable (anākhye), is the seat named Bhāsāśvarī, born from the syllable *?*. Thus, the group of six faces is [described] in brief; the rest is obtained from the mouth of the Guru. In this way, the face of Chva.
Furthermore, what is the Blessed Goddess like? The goddess has thirty-six arms and bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*).

I shall describe her weapons; I will tell them to you exactly as they are: the sword (*khaḍga*), the skull-cup (*kapāla*), the trident (*triśūla*), the bow (*miva*), the staff with a skull-topped end (*khaṭvāṅga*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), the noose (*pāśa*), the lute (*vīṇā*), the animal (*paśu*), the serpent (*phaṇi*), the double-headed serpent (*dviphaṇi*), the thunderbolt (*vajra*), the mallet (*mudgara*), and the arrow (*vāṇa*).

The bow, the discus, the tomara-weapon, the lotus, and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*)— these, O fair-faced goddess, are said to be on the right side. The mace, the dagger, the divine conch, the mirror, the scissors, the *cāliṅga*, the severed head,
the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), the mace, the spear, the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), the skull-bowl, and the hair-tuft, as well as the fierce weapon (*caṇḍāstra*)— these she carries.
The Pāśupatas, however, hold an axe in their hand; in the southeast (Āgneyī) direction, the Vāruṇa, Abhaya, and Prasāda mudrās are said, O Goddess, to be in the west (Vāruṇī);
and that which is called the Vāṅgamā is in the northwest (Mārutī), with thirty-six serpent-like weapons.
It maintains the thirty-six principles: earth, water, fire, air, and space; sound, touch, taste, form, and smell; speech, hands, anus, genitals, and feet;
ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose; mind, intellect, ego, and primordial matter (pradhāna) consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa); as well as the Puruṣa, Yama, and Niyama.
Rāga, Kāla, Vidya, and Māyā; Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva—thus there are thirty-six principles (tattvas). 36.

And the thirty-six weapons shall be described; thus they are fully explained, and one should hold them with the hands. Having many forms and many arms, they are indeed innumerable and beyond measure. From this [source], the form is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), yet it is manifested as having parts. "Ṭhaḥ" is the very [mantra]. Seated upon a lotus throne, they are worshipped; behind that, the *preta* is said to be situated.
Behind that, there should be Indra-muṇḍa, and behind Indra, Brahmaka;
behind that, Viṣṇu-muṇḍa should be, and behind Viṣṇu, Rudraka.
Behind that, however, seven [deities] should be worshipped, including Sādākṣa and Muṇḍa;
O Goddess, one should worship these five great pretas behind that.

The heart of Mahāpadma and the *seka* (consecration) are free from transformation; and upon its back, in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), dwells the *preta*. By the word *preta*, there is the state of *Sadāśiva* for that [being]. This is for the purpose of embracing [the disciple] by Indra.
In the middle, one should taste that which has entered into Brahman; having worshipped the skull of Brahman, it is known. || 2 ||
In the center, the mental fluctuations have dissolved; resting together with Viṣṇu’s severed head, it is to be worshipped. || 3 ||
The cause of all things is that alone; nothing else proceeds forth. It is the skull of Rudra, worshipped by the skull of Rudra.
By always maintaining a seat and a simple livelihood, one becomes the Lord of beings; thus, the Lord Muṇḍa is to be worshipped. || 5 ||

20a) As it was said, the mantra "sthala" [is recited]; Sadāśiva is the one to be worshipped as the "Muṇḍa" (the Headless/Topmost). On his back, the Goddess is to be worshipped; what is her true nature? She is the supreme state of equanimity (*samarasa*). By this [means], she is not [separate] from the river... [or: by this, she is not... (Note: The final portion of the fragment appears to be a corrupted or highly elliptical phrase concerning the non-duality of the deity and the cosmic flow.)

O Goddess Prabhasarati, whose own nature is the ground of peerless tranquility, I protect you who have come for refuge. Homage to these five hundred [deities] by means of this [mantra]. One should worship the goddesses according to their bodily intention; however, one should worship them with the mantra at the time of the ritual.

The Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). *Ākāśa* (Space) is *pha*; *Vāta* (Wind) is *ra*; *Teja* (Fire) is *o*; *Āpa* (Water) is *ma*; *Pṛthivī* (Earth) is *la*. *Ojā*, *Apūka*, *Amīkā*, and *Kāmarūpā* are yellow; *Ākāśa* is yellow. *Pūrṇagiri* is *bhaga*; *Vāta* is *Jālandhara*; *Teja* is *Oḍyāna*; *Āpa* is *Piṇḍa*; [and] *Yogapīṭha*.
The body is earth, the skin water, the blood fire, the bones wind, and the roar space;
thus it is fivefold. (20b)

They flash forth. "Five-colored"—this refers to the determination of the five lumps (*pañcapiṇḍa*) and the mantra; thus indeed, one should worship according to the principle of conjunction. For the sake of liberation, a white lotus is used; for the sake of enjoyment, a red one is prescribed; for the sake of desire, a yellow-colored one; and for killing, a black one is prescribed. This is the intended meaning. [She is] Karaṅkiṇī and Krodhinī, and likewise...

Or rather, Saṅkarṣaṇī is worshipped on the left side; now listen, O Goddess, regarding the right side. The pervasion of the year consists of the forms of the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *aḥ*. The pervasion of Fire (*agni*) consists of the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *bha*. The pervasion of the Moon (*soma*) consists of the letters beginning with *ma* and ending with *sa*. This is it.
The arising of Māyā and A*rasyā; Karaṅkiṇī is the form, Śakti is Saṃkarṣaṇī, and the noose is the power (pāśa-śakti).
According to this principle, one should worship by way of the left path (vāmamārga). Khecarī, Lelihānā, the third, and Catuṣbhairavī are on the right.

The supreme power is Lelihānā; that Bhairavī is the supreme power. Thus, one should worship the supreme, the non-supreme, the supreme-and-non-supreme, and the primordial supreme in the center of the two goddesses previously mentioned, on the path of the right.
She is to be worshipped; at the beginning, she is Trailokyamohanī, who deludes the three worlds. And the second is Jayadrathā, who is affectionate toward her children. (2)
Again, the goddess Aṅgiras said: || 3 ||
By the fourth [chapter], there is the accomplishment of the Vātyadhika, as well as the secret convention and the Fortune of Accomplishment (Siddhilakṣmī) in the Jayadratha [Tantra]. || 5 ||

One should take up the name [of the deity] called E. O Great Goddess, listen now to something else regarding the past and the future. I shall describe the worship situated in the lineage of the mouth: Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka are to be worshipped; Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka are the two [aspects of] prāṇa and apāna; the Guru and Īśvara are the form [Ā].
The expansion of the letter *A* is a spark of consciousness, shimmering with the color of a white lotus.
At the beginning, when that [expansion] has spread forth, the Goddesses are worshipped. This was previously taught by the Goddess; it is conjoined with the twelve Goddesses.
One should avoid the meditation on the twelve Goddesses. She has five faces and eight arms.

21b) Placing her foot upon the earth, holding a lotus and a severed head; a book and the gesture of granting fearlessness in her hands, and a skull-bowl shines in her hand—this eighth [hand] is proclaimed; this is the twelfth visualization (dhyāna). These...

There are twelve months; then the twelve digits (kalās), and the number of the elements and sages. Again, the Supreme Goddess should worship the six syllables; she is dark, terrifying, fierce, and adorned with a garland of skulls.
She has one face, three eyes, wears a garland of severed heads, and possesses four arms.
She holds a shaven head, a lotus, a blazing noose, and a goad;
or alternatively, a sword and a small dagger—these six are to be meditated upon as the *mudrās*.
Furthermore, one should worship the pledges (samayas) right there;
she is established with five faces, ten arms, and three eyes.
Seated upon a lotus throne amidst the hungry ghosts, radiant and situated in the center of a moon mandala,
these goddesses grant long life and accomplish desired results according to one's wish.
One should worship Śaṅkhinī and Śivādūtī on the left and the right;
having worshipped all these, one should then worship the Supreme Goddess.
Thus ends the third chapter, the commentary on the procedure for worship, in the *Śrīkālasaṅkarṣaṇīmata*, consisting of twenty-four thousand verses.
The Śrī Devī said:
How does the Caruka and the Saṃpradāya come about from mouth to mouth? What is the discourse, what is the end of the discourse, and how is the station established?
O Lord of Gods, O Master, tell me how these places [are established];
and this as well.
The Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim my secret which is difficult to obtain;
it is the supreme life-force of the Yoginīs, which has never been told to anyone before.
The superior, inferior, and middling varieties, as well as palāṇḍu,
garlic, gañjana, viśvakṣāra, harāmbu, and bhadra.
The stalk of grain, clarified butter, the menstrual flower, the sacrificial pap of fish and raw meat, and the most excellent liquor, Hālāhala—these sixteen are proclaimed. (16)
The primary [offering] is a charu-oblation for thirteen [deities]: mind, ear, eye, tongue, nose, the faculties of cognition, the ego-sense, and the state of mind-transcending.
Compassion, suspicion, fear, shame, discernment, secrecy, and noble lineage—[these are the qualities of a spy]. || 16 ||

And others [practice] bathing, movement, and [meditation on] the heart as the navel of the bulb; the subtle channel from the center of the tortoise, the upward-facing moon; and the supportless state at the end of the *nāda* for those who have restrained the senses and mind.
The primary positions:
the new moon (amāvāsyā) is honored as long as the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipadā) remains;
one should worship the fire at the end of the fifteenth day (pañcadaśamī).
From the new moon until the end of the first day is the *ruka*;
likewise, from the full moon until the new moon is the *prati* in direct order (*anuloma*).
O Yogin, listen to this one thing regarding the worship of Kṛṣṇapūrṇā. Hereafter I shall explain the ritual procedure; now listen.
Whatever artifice there may be, such as a boat, a staff,
or a liquid, that could kill the mind— therein one should not consume "great meat."

"Taraṇḍam," "taraṇḍām," and "daṇḍam. On the left path, the wind is the form; the letter *ta* is the color of the boat (*taraṇḍa*). On the right path, fire is the essential nature; the letter *ra* is the form in the middle of the staff (*daṇḍa*). Why is that? The form of the digit (*kalā*) is melted. One should strike the mind in that place. One should consume human flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*) and other things as well. 1.

The ears, skin, belly, and tongue—these are the vomit, devoid of duality. He should not consume meat that is impure due to the wind of the vital breath (*kalāpavana*). He does not hear sound; he sees form; the tongue tastes; and the heart grasps. Devoid of duality means being free from the two; he abandons all of this.
By practicing yoga day after day, one consumes the essence of the *samarasavikāra*; one becomes ageless and immortal, and possesses cattle. (2) [In the] foundation of the bulb (*kandādhāra*).

The tongue that speaks with joy, reaching as far as the root-support (*kandādhāra*), is the *lambikā*; it is nectar. One should drink from the *lambikā* and perform [the practice], while avoiding [what is contrary]. [One should] [protect] the *lambikā*. [One should] [restrain] the senses.

And one should consume it. A "pala" refers to an egg; [the substance] from the bulbous base (*kandādhāra*) up to the "twelve-finger limit" (*dvādaśānta*)—or rather, one becomes undecaying and immortal.
Likewise, by that measure, one should take garlic (*laśuna*).
But how could one who is awake and smelling the stench bring forth a humming sound? And as for the universal sacrificial pap (caru) situated within the submarine fire (vāḍavānala)? 6.

The meaning is that where there is the eclipse of the moon and the sun, one should bring forth the excrement (*purīṣa*). This is the *viśvagni-caru*. For what reason is there the swallowing of the moon and the sun? On the path of the left (*vāmamārga*), by means of the *pūraka* [breathing technique], the touch of the wind [should occur].
Thus, when the eclipse of the moon and the sun has been effected, one should bring forth the excrement there into the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*). || 7 ||
The water-wheel of the river and the [fluid] of the moon have just now been drained; from where could one obtain the water of Śiva, which is like a camel in the throat?
The Kuṇḍalinī has caused the channels (nāḍīs) to flow; the husk of the grain is then polished there.
One should offer the sacrificial oblations with flowers. The sun is the blood, the moon is the semen, the sphere is the wind; Śiva is the male, and Śakti is the female.

24b) Form (rūpa) causes the abode of the delusion of Śiva and Śakti to revolve; one's own true nature (svarūpa) is attained. Having performed the offering of the flower of the womb (yoni-puṣpa), and having offered the instrument of oblation, when the three impurities (mala-traya) have been sacrificed, let it move within the vessel of nectar (amṛta-kaṅkava).

One should extract the phlegm (*śleṣman*). Generally, [the energy] situated above is the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*), perfectly peaceful, full with the essence of the bliss of nectar (*amṛtānandarasena*), O God... [of] those two...
until the specific sacrifice (*viśeṣayāga*) and the threatening [gesture] (*tarjana*), and because of the moon... and that from which...

Since he [is the one] who, having subdued the regions of form (*rūpāyatanas*), rests upon the mud-free [ground], and having dissolved all activity, would crush the [remaining] moment; [this is] slander (*paiśunya*). Thus, the staff (*daṇḍa*) is thirty-six finger-breadths long.

The reality (*bhūta*) is situated as the mother; from that, the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) arise. That is the life-force staff (*prāṇadaṇḍa*), and the life-force (*prāṇa*) is the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
The two eyes do not move from the center of the eyebrows; there the yogi is intent on practice, but not one who is ostentatious—this is the meaning. || 13 ||
Where the sky is pure and where that which is established is without support,
there the yogi finds rest, but not the consumption of *hālāhala* poison.
The yogi meditates upon the *hālāhala* oblation as the sky, the space, and likewise the twelve-finger limit (*dvādaśānta*) which is without support; thus the mind transcends, O Yogin. 14.
The gods and asuras dwell within the left channel and the right channel;
that alone is the vessel of the goddesses, and no other whatsoever.

On the left is the god, on the right the asura; he brings about the state of being. There, the form of Nanda is obtained through the grace of the Guru. By the power of Śakti, the central channel (madhyamā nāḍī) is filled with the splendor of Bhairava. One should consume that thread and the wine, but not otherwise.

25b) Therefore, one should not drink the morning juice produced from grapes [or] from hunger. And desiring to cook, by means of the application of the triangular base of power (*śaktimūlaka*), the essence is drunk and the impurity is consumed.

The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall speak again:
Gayā is the first channel (nāḍī); Gayā is Suṣumnā and Kuṇḍalinī.
The essence of the supreme art (kalāvararasa) would be twelve and eight [parts]; divided twelvefold, it is six in the heart and likewise six. 6.
That which is situated above is called the Pitṛpāka; it consists of six Pitṛpātas. In the Devamāna there are six, and in the Devayāna there are six Devayānas. 6.
Thus, eighteen are proclaimed. || 18 ||
It is held that there are six hundred and sixty *tāla*-cavities; these are said to belong to the Sun (*sūrya*).
With six [cavities], and with two more, the third is the *suṣumnā*. One who sings the *ojas* of the eight [cavities] therein shall not undergo birth again. Thus indeed. Again...

The ritual of recitation and mastery is performed according to the Sūtra-mātṛkā. One should have a five-colored [image] made with the five jewels and rice. One should grind the rice powder into a paste and knead it into the form of a womb (yoni).
In this case, a hexagon should be drawn. The hexagon is the heart; there, one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is obtained.
A womb (*yoni*) is placed in the center. The womb is the solar orb, and outside of that is a square.
The square consists of the *ojā* and *puṭā*. With two lines on the left and right, there are the two, *prāṇa* and *apāna*. [Two].

And two [units] are given. Śiva and Śakti are above; one should join that circle, and half of that circle is the form of Māyā. The wise one should perform the ritual action provided with banners (*patākā*) and arches (*toraṇa*). Regarding the arch: the pole of the boat (*taraṇḍadaṇḍa*), the banner, and the twelve ends. Another is the swing-pavilion (*ādolālaya*); and the [five] rays are fivefold.

Kuṇḍalinī is fivefold. The banner [is seen] in the Abdalā; this is the illustration. The flag is the five causes. Kuṇḍalinī is fivefold: by means of inhalation (pūraka) and exhalation (pāta), her own nature is attained. In the hexagon are the twelve suns of the Goddess. 12.

Śivā and the others [are worshipped] in the center, as is Kṛṣodarī. One should worship the Power of Breath (Prāṇaśakti) in the square in the middle; one should worship two each of the goddesses Vāmā and Dakṣiṇā. Śivādūtī is in the [central] space; one should worship the two full of compassion in the middle.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the commentary on the Kuṇḍamuṇḍalā [section], in the venerable Kālasaṃkarṣaṇīmata.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain [this]:
the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is Brahmabila; the deity is the thirty-two-fold [Vidyā];
then, beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, there are the three girdles (*mekhalā*).

Having formed [the mudrās] of the Moon, Sun, and Fire; and of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—with one, two, three, and four fingers respectively—[one should know that] Viṣṇu is the second, Rudra the third, and Brahmā the fourth; thus is the girdle (mekhalā). 27b)
Having made the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) very beautiful, I shall explain it to you as it is:
in the fire-offering (homa), one should use [substances] combined with bilva fruits and the like.
O lady of excellent hips, the wise one should cause it to be made for the purpose of enjoyment. || 3 ||
The red flower of the *adaka* tree, joined with blood—for the sake of subjugation, success is obtained; *svāhā*, O Blessed Śiva! || 4 ||
When great fear has arisen and a vast conflict has broken out, [one should offer] *kusuma* with the *brahmavṛkṣa*. (28a)
Now listen to the procedure for killing:
at night, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) in a cremation ground with mercury as prescribed.
At a single tree by the river, [the practitioner],
desiring success,
should offer eight fuel-sticks and cakes together with clarified butter, honey, and milk, combined with a thousand [recitations] and accompanied by the Mahātala [mantra].
Having performed one hundred and eight recitations of the *māgma* and the *tritaśāni*, I shall explain the second [rite]; one should then commence the fire-ritual (*agnikarman*).
Having prepared twenty-seven small packets of alkali (palakṣāra),
the wise one should cause them to be offered as oblations half by half every day;
first, the mudrās should be presented, as well as the three deities.
O Goddess, thus has the triad of fire-rites been described. Now, as for the signs and characteristics:
[the fire] is smoky, blue, full, and described as having sparks.
Jvālā and Tejasvatī, and indeed... [the rest of the verse].
28b) Unclear,
deluding, and always carried away.
By joining the thumb with the ring finger, one performs the supreme rite of subjugation;
by joining the thumb with the little finger, it becomes effective for the rite of eradication.
By means of the application of the five fingers, one endures all desires;
such is the characteristic of this which is to be told to Vakṣe.
Furthermore, I shall again proclaim [the teaching] concerning the Yoginī who has certainly heated the life-force of others.
One who desires worship, by mounting a vehicle on Jyeṣṭhā, shall obtain their desired objects; O Goddess, whatever vehicle one contemplates, that very vehicle they shall obtain.

The eldest [portion] is the southern quarter; that is the most excellent form. The direction of the vehicle is its southern part, reaching to the venerable feet. Now, indeed, its cord consists of silver, copper, and water. The third is iron... [and so forth].

Having bowed to the pedestal (pīṭhikā), on its back is the pair [of verses] as previously described. There, one should worship the sixteen [deities] of the southern direction, beginning with *A*. Whose...
He causes [the deceased] to go during the night on the eighth day of the month, and then at the change of the seasons.

The illustrious Bhairava said:
I shall now fully explain the *tilaka*, as well as the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the ritual practice (*sādhana*),
along with collyrium (*añjana*), pills (*guṭikā*), and so forth, for the purpose of subjugation and increase.
O Goddess, there is nothing that this vessel of the netherworld (pātāla) cannot accomplish.

[The mantra is] "He kā karṇā te. Having made a fine powder of pus, *gurucana*, *rodhra*, *pippilī*, *unthasana*, *śilā*, and white sandalwood, one should protect these at the junction of the night (*bhāyute*).
Having consecrated seven sesame seeds with mantras, the world comes under one's control; through these, even unthought-of riches always arise for that person from the royal assembly.
I shall explain the sequence that exists in the forest of food together with blood.
The wise one should perform this entire [rite] for the sake of the sacrificer.
Here we shall explain the terminology: "gosāraṇa" is well-known [as a type of incense]; "kuṅkuma" is well-known [as saffron];
by the word "candra" is meant camphor; "malaya" refers to sandalwood;
"rasa" is placed upon the breast; "mṛganābhi" is musk; "akuṇḍagolaka" arises from the union of Śiva and Śakti; it is self-existent (*svayaṃbhu*).
Kusuma. Bhaga, born from the first... This entire [work]...
accompanied by the power of... [unclear].
34a) O four-faced one,
by the sound of *laṃ* and *kṣa*, [the obstacle] perishes; and in the land of Kāśmīra, you abandon them.

One should worship the four-faced, fierce [deity] during the dark fortnight. Now I shall proclaim another mantra for an empty house, by which this world is deluded: it consists of the one called Kuṇḍalā joined with the Yoni, or else with the Giver (Dāyaka).
It is to be given in two ways: first, *revahauṃ haḥ*, and then the three-fold group (*trivarga*) for the bliss of the great Mantra-Yoginīs.

It remains. In one place, the mantra *haḥ huṃ huṃ*—these three syllables—with the water of Viṣṇurasa, [is used] for the vomiting of poison. The reflection (*bimba*) is joined with the water, being struck and liquefied; the vehicle (*vāhana*) is also liquefied. On its back, having assumed the form of the directions, he utters the *hūṃ* syllable for you—this is the meaning. The bulb (*kanda*).

One should draw forth the twelve digits at the *dvādaśānta*; one should draw forth the Sun [and so on]. That which is throbbing and primordial, possessing all states of being, is so described. (ka 34b)
Connected. * * * * * * * * *? He was that...

One should speak of the lack of affection among fallen people;
there is much suffering and grief, as well as worship. All things beginning with the earth, the entire Brahmāṇḍa, including the moving and the unmoving.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva themselves—[even they] are satisfied by its end; such is the fruit of that primordial sacrifice.
Above that, Kālāgnirudra is worshipped, ending with Śiva;
likewise, there are the seven islands, the oceans, and the fourteen worlds.
O Śivayogin, the fruit of that primordial sacrifice is such that even the killing of a Brahmin, the killing of a cow, or the murder of an embryo shall be destroyed.
The guru, mother, father, brother, and kinsmen are everywhere;
having caused all sins to perish, one should indeed resort to the primordial sacrifice.
The fruit of his enjoyment and liberation is good fortune accompanied by wealth;
the three-eyed Lord Hara shall dwell with him eternally in the world of Rudra.
Sixty million [times] ten thousand [offerings] arise from a proud maiden;
or else, the fruit of that for those performing the initial sacrifice is like that of a horse-slayer.
35b) Having extracted each one from the form of the sand-heap up to the end of Śiva and above, even seven hundred koṭis [of times].
The jackals devour that [remnant] as long as the earth and the sun endure;
through the desire for the first sacrifice, it reaches its end.
Those who revile the guru, whoever they may be; those who disparage the mantras, whoever they may be;
those who disparage the sacred seats (pīṭha), and whoever would disparage the yoginīs.
And whoever reviles the heroes, or those who defile Śiva and Śakti,
shall be cooked in a terrible hell until the dissolution of the earth.
From the realm of Raurava up to the state of Sadāśiva,
he who is poor and destitute here [in this world] will, like others, bring about the destruction of his lineage.
The ten borders are wiped clean by meat;
[he] is devoted to the mantra and meditation of his devotees.
